tagline.text: A hilltop garden park in Puerto Princesa that grew out of a small bakery

budget.label: Budget
budget.text: About ₱200~800 (per person, including snacks and souvenirs)

children.text: Baker's Hill began as a small bakery selling hopia and has grown into a complex of gardens, statues, a playground and a small animal area on a hill north of Puerto Princesa. Admission is free, and it makes an easy stop on a city tour for photos and snacks.
Baker's Hill sits on a hill along Mitra Road, about
8km

north of downtown Puerto Princesa, the main city of Palawan. It started as a small bakery famous for hopia, and as customers kept coming, gardens and statues were added to the surrounding grounds until it became what it is today. Now the bakery, restaurants, souvenir shops and lawn gardens all share one compound, making it something of a mini theme park.

The most eye-catching feature is the life-size statues scattered around the grounds. Figures modeled on famous people and cartoon characters, a calesa (horse carriage) replica and a tiger statue stand among neatly trimmed shrubs and cobblestone paths, so almost any corner makes a photo. There is also a children's playground, a plant nursery, a small area where you can see animals such as peacocks, and an oriental-style garden, which is why many families visit. The statue lineup can change over time, so check what is actually there when you arrive.
Entry is reported to be free, and opening hours are usually listed as roughly
to

, though sources differ slightly. Some descriptions also mention a viewing deck overlooking the city and the sea. Keep in mind that this is a commercial attraction rather than a natural sight; it is best treated as a relaxed stop on a Puerto Princesa city tour, not a destination to expect too much from. One more thing to know before you go: the fees, hours and facilities of Baker's Hill are described a little differently on each travel site and blog, so rather than trusting a single source, check the latest reviews and opening hours on a map app as well. Google Maps carries more than 3,000 reviews, which helps you gauge how the place is today. Just looking around usually takes 1–2 hours, and a meal plus shopping will keep you longer.

People often visit when they have half a day to spare between an underground river tour and Honda Bay island hopping, or to buy hopia and cashew nuts to take home before flying out. It is a regular stop on Puerto Princesa city tour itineraries, including among Korean travelers.

This is the bakery where Baker's Hill began. Hopia is the signature item, and it also sells Filipino breads and sweets such as ensaymada, crinkles and ube bread. Many reviewers say you can watch the bread being baked. Hopia comes with several kinds of filling, so ask the staff for a recommendation.

Statues modeled on famous people and cartoon characters stand throughout the garden. There are also photo spots such as a tiger statue and a calesa (horse carriage) replica. With children, a full circuit takes more than
30 minutes

Trimmed trees, lawns, shaded gazebos and outdoor tables line the grounds. It is a good place to rest in the shade during the hot part of the day, and the outdoor tables have sungka, a traditional Filipino board game, that you can try. The complex is on a hill, so there are a few ups and downs between areas; take your time.

A playground and a small area where you can see animals such as peacocks draw many families with children. The animal area is not large, so do not expect zoo-level attractions. When the sun is strong, bring hats and water for the kids.

Because the complex is on a hill, it is described as having a deck that looks toward the city and the sea. On a clear afternoon it is a pleasant spot for photos in a cool breeze. The view depends on the weather and on any construction, so check on site.

You can have lunch or a snack at the restaurants inside the complex. Reviews often mention noodle dishes such as pancit served as merienda (afternoon snack), and a news report also described unusual local specialties such as tamilok. Menus and prices change often.

Besides bread, shops sell cashew nuts, snacks, handicrafts and souvenirs such as T-shirts. Palawan cashews are a popular gift among Korean travelers. Check price tags and pick items with good packaging.

items.title: 1–2 hour route
items.subtitle: A short stop during a city tour

children.text: Get off at the parking lot or entrance and visit the bakery first to look over the hopia and other breads.
Walk the garden and statue area and take photos. If you have children, spend time at the playground.
Go up to the viewing deck to look toward the city, then enjoy snacks and a drink at a shaded outdoor table.
Buy hopia and cashews at the souvenir shop and head out. Buying gifts last keeps your luggage easier to carry.
Late morning or late afternoon is less scorching. The busy hours for tour groups depend on local conditions, so plan with some slack.

items.title: Puerto Princesa full-day route
items.subtitle: One stop on a city tour

children.text: Leave your downtown hotel and look around the city sights and market.
Head north along Mitra Road to Baker's Hill for lunch and a stroll through the gardens.
Continue to a nearby ranch-style attraction or to Honda Bay plans. Check each facility for operating status and entrance fees.
Return to the city and have dinner in the waterfront dining area.
City tour packages often include Baker's Hill. Check the package description to see whether admission is included.

items.title: Flying from Manila to Puerto Princesa

children.text: Direct flights from Manila (NAIA) to Puerto Princesa International Airport (PPS) take about
1 hour 40 minutes
. Depending on the airline and season, there are several flights a day.
From the airport to Baker's Hill it is roughly
8km
in a straight line, so a tricycle, taxi or hotel pickup gets you there easily.
Flight schedules and fares change often, so check the latest information before booking.
A taxi or Grab from downtown is generally said to take about
20–30 minutes
, depending on traffic. Check the meter or the fare shown in the app.

The official guide lists a tricycle from the airport or downtown at about ₱300 for up to three people; in practice the fare is negotiated. Getting a ride back can be hard, so it is safer to arrange waiting time or book a round trip.

The Puerto Princesa city tourism office (official) says to take a jeepney or multicab bound for Sta. Monica along the national highway, listing a fare of about ₱16 per person. Blogs also describe riding an Irawan-bound jeepney, getting off at the Mitra Road junction and switching to a tricycle. Fares change over the years, so confirm with the driver before boarding.
A rental car or a car with a driver is efficient if you combine Baker's Hill with sights along the northern coast.
Many travel agency city tour packages include Baker's Hill. Whether admission and meals are included differs by package.
The attraction is mostly gardens and outdoor facilities, so weather matters a great deal. Puerto Princesa is generally dry from
November–May
and rainy from
June–October
During the day, early morning or late afternoon is more comfortable for walking than the midday sun. Weekends bring more local families, and many reviewers say weekdays are calmer.
Around New Year, Philippine public holidays and school vacations, visitor numbers can rise sharply, so we recommend going early in the morning then.

The outdoor garden gets muddy on rainy days, so bring an umbrella and check the forecast

The complex has restaurants and cafes, which makes it a good place for lunch or an afternoon snack. The menu centers on Filipino noodle dishes, simple meals, bread and drinks, and menus and prices change often. Some notices say a corkage fee applies if you bring outside food, so ask at the entrance. Seats can run short at weekend lunchtime when local families come, so it helps to arrive a little early.

Most travelers do not stay here but in downtown Puerto Princesa, near the airport, or near the underground river and Honda Bay. Because it is close to the city, you can visit in half a day from your hotel. Downtown has Korean restaurants and seafood restaurants, so dinner is easy to sort out in the city.

After Baker's Hill, the usual plan is to return to the city for seafood or continue to Honda Bay activities. Downtown has clusters of money changers, convenience stores and pharmacies, which is handy for stocking up. Gifts such as Palawan cashews and dried mango, besides bread and sweets, are also available at city markets, so compare prices.
Check first whether it is included in your city tour. If it is, you do not need to come separately.
Bakery prices may differ between shops, so buy gifts last. Hopia is sometimes sold by the pack.
You need a hat, sunscreen and water in the heat of the day. Find a shaded table to rest.
Photos are best in the morning or on weekdays when fewer people are around. A line can form in front of the statues.
If you ride a tricycle up, arrange your ride back in advance or check whether you can call a car with an app.
With children, plan a short visit focused on the playground and the animal area.
Bread and sweets spoil easily in the heat, so check the packaging and expiry date of gifts you take home.
Opening hours differ between sources. If you plan to go late, check before you visit.
Carry plenty of small bills. Tricycles and small shops may not accept cards.
If you plan several stops in Puerto Princesa in one day, putting Baker's Hill at the end of the morning or at the start of the afternoon makes a natural route.
This is a commercial attraction, not a natural sight. Fees, hours and facilities can change, so check the latest information before you go.
Reviews mention limited parking, so go early in peak season.
The stairs and cobblestone paths in the garden can be awkward in sandals or flip-flops, so wear comfortable shoes.
Keep your belongings with you in crowded spots, and do not take your eyes off children near play facilities.
Sudden rain is common in the rainy season, so bring an umbrella or raincoat.
Do not climb on the statues or the animal area, and do not feed the animals.
Some areas may close for repairs or events, so check before you visit.
Downtown is about
20–30 minutes
away by car. You can combine it with the market, the cathedral and the waterfront restaurant area.
This is a departure point for island hopping to the north. Many travelers combine it with a stop at Baker's Hill. Check departure times and fares locally.
Palawan's signature World Heritage site. Entry permits must be arranged in advance, and it usually takes a day of its own.
One blog described a ranch and viewpoint facility about
5 minutes
by car from Baker's Hill. Check on site whether it is open.
